206	\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
207	\label{sec:irreducible}
208	
209	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
210	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
211	
212	\begin{itemize}
213	\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95)---a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
214	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
215	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
216	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
217	\end{itemize}
218	
219	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
220	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines---even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
221	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
222	This is not a model failure but a representation ceiling: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
223	
224	These 2 irreducible errors establish a practical accuracy ceiling of $1 - 2/1190 = 99.83\%$ for the \texttt{exception\_only} condition on this dataset, suggesting that further improvements would require either supplementary trace signals or modifications to the input representation.

\label{sec:irreducible}

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.

\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines---even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ceiling: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

4	
5	We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.

7	Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution, providing a cleaner lens on what trace information actually contributes.

16	Because multiple passing solutions to the same problem produce identical (input, output) pairs in the \texttt{exception\_only} format---correct executions raise no exceptions, so the trace content is the same regardless of the solution's internal logic---the dataset contains duplicate rows.
17	Table~\ref{tab:dedup} reports the duplication rates across formats.
18	Train--test input overlap is zero (split by problem ID), so no information leakage occurs.
19	The high duplication in \texttt{exception\_only} does not affect our experimental conclusions: after deduplication the training set still contains 2,858 unique samples and the test set 607, providing sufficient coverage for the 591-problem benchmark.
20	The \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% duplicate inputs due to representation compactness; all confidence intervals treat samples as independent Bernoulli trials.
21	We report these statistics for transparency.

39	\subsection{Trace Representations}
40	
41	We define seven input conditions that systematically vary the trace information available to the model (Figure~\ref{fig:trace_overview}):
42	
43	\begin{itemize}
44	\item \texttt{no\_trace}: Source code and test input only; no execution information.
45	\item \texttt{full\_trace}: Complete line-by-line execution trace recording variable states at each step.
46	\item \texttt{VOTA} (Verdict-Oriented Trace Abstraction): Three compressed components---exception events, assertion-point comparisons, and loop compression summaries.
47	\item \texttt{exception\_only}: Only exception and error events extracted from the trace (e.g., \texttt{[ERROR] TypeError: ...}).
48	\item \texttt{ae\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected value pairs from the final comparison.
49	\item \texttt{loop\_only}: Only loop compression summaries (iteration counts and final variable states).
50	\item \texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information (exception events + loop compression).
51	\end{itemize}
52	
53	These conditions span a spectrum from no trace information (\texttt{no\_trace}) through maximally compressed signals (\texttt{exception\_only}) to the complete unfiltered trace (\texttt{full\_trace}).
54

56	\centering
57	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}
58	\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace. Each condition is paired with the same model to predict a pass/fail verdict. Accuracies shown are for Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B (seed=42, $N{=}1{,}190$).}
59	\label{fig:trace_overview}
60	\end{figure*}

62	\subsection{Models}
63	
64	We evaluate two instruction-tuned code LLMs at the 7B parameter scale:
65	
66	\begin{itemize}
67	\item \textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct} \citep{qwen2025coder}: Pretrained on 5.5T tokens. Serves as the primary model for all ablation experiments.
68	\item \textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \citep{deepseek2024coder}: Pretrained on 2T tokens. Used for cross-model validation to test whether findings generalize beyond a single model family.
69	\end{itemize}
70	
71	The two models differ primarily in pretraining data volume (5.5T vs.\ 2T tokens), providing a natural axis for evaluating whether trace signal utility is model-dependent \citep{dong2024composition}.
72	
73	\subsection{Training Setup}
74	
75	All conditions use identical training configurations to ensure fair comparison.
76	We apply LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} (rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05) to all linear layers and train for 3 epochs with batch size 4, gradient accumulation 8 (effective batch size 32), learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup and linear decay, warmup ratio 0.1, and weight decay 0.01.
77	The maximum sequence length is 2,048 tokens; input sequences exceeding this limit are truncated from the input content while preserving the complete verdict label.
78	Training wall-clock time ranges from 0.5 to 2.5 hours per condition on a single GPU, depending on trace format verbosity.
79	The primary seed is 42; seed robustness is evaluated with seeds 123 and 456 for the \texttt{exception\_only} condition.
80	
81	\subsection{Loss Ablation}
82	
83	To disentangle training signal quality from input signal quality, we introduce a \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} variant.
84	This condition uses the same full trace as input but computes loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace tokens during training (loss weight = 0 on trace positions).
85	If this variant improves over standard \texttt{full\_trace}, the improvement is attributable to \emph{gradient dilution}---trace tokens diluting the training signal without contributing to verdict prediction.
86	The remaining gap to VOTA is then attributable to \emph{information overload}---irrelevant trace content that the model must process at inference time.

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces---line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior---have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models.
Recent work has explored trace-augmented training for code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile}, execution-aware pretraining \citep{ding2024traced}, trace-based code understanding \citep{wang2025dcsh}, and self-training on trace chain-of-thought \citep{ni2024next}.
Yet a fundamental question remains open: \emph{which components of an execution trace actually matter?}

\citet{wang2025dcsh} found that no single trace representation consistently outperforms others on generation-oriented tasks, concluding that the utility of execution traces is task- and format-dependent.
However, their study focused on code generation and repair---tasks that require the model to simulate or reconstruct execution semantics.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---is a fundamentally different task type: it is a fault detection problem, not a generation problem.
Whether the same trace components matter for fault detection as for generation is unknown.

We present the first systematic study of what trace components drive verdict prediction performance.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} with model-generated solutions and execution traces, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components and evaluate each in isolation across two models: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct.

Our results reveal a striking finding: \textbf{exception events alone achieve near-perfect verdict prediction on Qwen (99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00, 3 seeds) and are the most effective component on DeepSeek, with 2/3 seeds matching Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the remaining seed (91.09\%) reflects LoRA initialization sensitivity rather than a signal limitation.}
Even the DeepSeek outlier seed (91.09\%) outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) and no-trace (73.36\%) by wide margins, confirming exception events as the dominant trace component across models.
In contrast, the full VOTA representation---which combines exception events with assertion-point and loop information---degrades by 14.96pp on DeepSeek.
Post-hoc analysis reveals the mechanism: the DeepSeek tokenizer produces longer sequences than Qwen for identical inputs, causing 91.7\% of VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window; the training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates the trace content, so the model trains on incomplete diagnostic information.

These results reframe verdict prediction as fault detection: the minimal sufficient signal is the exception event, a compact structured diagnostic moment that both models can interpret without deep trace reasoning.
We further decompose the gap between full trace and VOTA into two mechanisms---\emph{gradient dilution} (26\% of the gap) and \emph{information overload} (74\%)---showing that the primary bottleneck is not training signal quality but the presence of irrelevant trace content.

We note that the finding that exception events dominate verdict prediction is not itself surprising---exceptions are, by definition, fault indicators.
The novelty lies in three less obvious results: (1)~adding more trace information actively \emph{hurts} performance (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}), (2)~we quantify \emph{why} through a 26/74 gradient-dilution/information-overload decomposition, and (3)~the VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by tokenizer-driven trace truncation: the DeepSeek tokenizer causes the majority of VOTA training samples to exceed the context window (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}), truncating diagnostic trace content while preserving the verdict label.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exception signal transfer}: We show that exception events alone achieve 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 on Qwen (3 seeds) and 99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds, with one outlier at 91.09\% from LoRA initialization sensitivity; even the outlier exceeds VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
\item \textbf{Information density decomposition}: We decompose the full-trace-to-VOTA gap into gradient dilution (26\%) and information overload (74\%), identifying the primary bottleneck for trace-based prediction (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Component ablation reveals that Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) reach only 85.6\% (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

3	We evaluate our trace preprocessing pipeline across two research questions:
4	(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models of different capability?
5	(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component to verdict prediction accuracy?

9	\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
10	\label{sec:cross_model}
11	
12	To test whether exception-based trace compression transfers across model families, we compare Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct under four input conditions: \texttt{exception\_only} (Tier~1 exception events), VOTA (exception + assertion-point + loop compression), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete execution trace), and \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only).

33	
34	Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} reveals a striking asymmetry.
35	Under \texttt{exception\_only}, Qwen achieves 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 across three seeds, while DeepSeek shows a bimodal pattern: seeds 42 and 456 both achieve 99.33\% (gap = 0.50pp), while seed 123 yields 91.09\% (gap = 8.74pp), attributable to suboptimal LoRA initialization (fail recall = 70.5\% vs.\ 100\% for other seeds).
36	Even the outlier seed outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp, confirming exception events as the most effective component across models.
37	Under VOTA, the gap widens to 14.96pp: DeepSeek drops to 84.45\% while Qwen remains at 99.41\%.
38	Post-hoc tokenizer analysis reveals a confound: measured on the training set using each model's tokenizer, the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}759 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}908 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
39	The VOTA training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates the trace content (input), so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the vast majority of the dataset.
40	The 14.96pp gap thus reflects both model capability differences and training-time trace truncation; the two factors cannot be disentangled in the current design.
41	However, a post-hoc group analysis provides directional evidence: partitioning DeepSeek VOTA test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}0.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class of the truncated group (fail recall $=$ 31.23\%).
42	In contrast, the \texttt{exception\_only} condition is unaffected by truncation because exception-based inputs are short enough to fit within the context window for both tokenizers, making its cross-model comparison clean.
43	Per-class analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}) reveals the mechanism: DeepSeek VOTA achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}---in contrast to Qwen VOTA, which achieves 100\% fail recall.

All experiments use our trace--verdict dataset (\S\ref{sec:dataset}) with $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals unless stated otherwise.
Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all cross-condition differences reported below are significant at $p{<}0.0001$ unless noted otherwise.

\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

To test whether exception-based trace compression transfers across model families, we compare Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct under four input conditions: \texttt{exception\_only} (Tier~1 exception events), VOTA (exception + assertion-point + loop compression), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete execution trace), and \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-2.5-7B} & \textbf{DeepSeek-6.7B} & \textbf{Gap} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}\% & 99.33\%$^\dag$ & 0.50pp \\
VOTA & 99.41\% & 84.45\% & 14.96pp \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & 99.41\%$^\S$ & --- & --- \\
full\_trace & 81.76\% & 79.16\% & 2.60pp \\
no\_trace & 75.13\% & 73.36\% & 1.77pp \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & 71.51\% & 71.51\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Cross-model accuracy ($N{=}1{,}190$). Qwen CIs: exception\_only [99.58, 100.00], VOTA [98.82, 99.83], full\_trace [79.70, 83.90], no\_trace [72.77, 77.48]; DeepSeek CIs: full\_trace [76.80, 81.30], VOTA [82.60, 86.40], no\_trace [70.80, 75.70]. $^\dag$DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} 3-seed results: 99.33\% (seeds 42, 456; CI [98.82, 99.75]) and 91.09\% (seed 123; CI [89.40, 92.60]); seed 123 is a LoRA initialization outlier (fail recall = 70.5\% vs.\ 100\%). $^\S$VOTA\_no\_ae evaluated on Qwen only; CI [98.90, 99.80].}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} reveals a striking asymmetry.
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, Qwen achieves 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 across three seeds, while DeepSeek shows a bimodal pattern: seeds 42 and 456 both achieve 99.33\% (gap = 0.50pp), while seed 123 yields 91.09\% (gap = 8.74pp), attributable to suboptimal LoRA initialization (fail recall = 70.5\% vs.\ 100\% for other seeds).
Even the outlier seed outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp, confirming exception events as the most effective component across models.
Under VOTA, the gap widens to 14.96pp: DeepSeek drops to 84.45\% while Qwen remains at 99.41\%.
Post-hoc tokenizer analysis reveals a confound: measured on the training set using each model's tokenizer, the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}759 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}908 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The VOTA training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates the trace content (input), so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the vast majority of the dataset.
The 14.96pp gap thus reflects both model capability differences and training-time trace truncation; the two factors cannot be disentangled in the current design.
However, a post-hoc group analysis provides directional evidence: partitioning DeepSeek VOTA test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}0.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class of the truncated group (fail recall $=$ 31.23\%).
In contrast, the \texttt{exception\_only} condition is unaffected by truncation because exception-based inputs are short enough to fit within the context window for both tokenizers, making its cross-model comparison clean.
Per-class analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}) reveals the mechanism: DeepSeek VOTA achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}---in contrast to Qwen VOTA, which achieves 100\% fail recall.

The \texttt{no\_trace} baseline confirms that source code alone provides limited signal (75.13\% for Qwen, 73.36\% for DeepSeek), only marginally above majority-class guessing (71.51\%).

Seed robustness diverges sharply across models.
Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical accuracy of 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$, $n{=}3$, exactly two errors each).
DeepSeek shows a bimodal pattern ($n{=}3$): seeds 42 and 456 both achieve 99.33\% (8 errors each, fail recall = 100\%), while seed 123 yields 91.09\% (fail recall = 70.5\%), consistent with LoRA initialization sensitivity on the smaller model.
Because the \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% duplicate inputs (607 unique out of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), the reported CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials.
Under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's two errors yield 99.67\% accuracy (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]), confirming that the result is robust to the effective sample size.

\subsection{Component Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}

We decompose the VOTA pipeline into individual components on Qwen-2.5-7B (seed=42).
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} arranges conditions into a two-tier hierarchy: Tier~1 signals (\texttt{ae\_only}, \texttt{exception\_only}) that individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy, and Tier~2 signals (\texttt{loop\_only}) that provide moderate improvement over the no-trace baseline.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Components} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Tier} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & assertion-point & \textbf{99.92} & [99.75, 100.00] & 1 \\
exception\_only & exception events & 99.83 & [99.58, 100.00] & 1 \\
VOTA & exc+ae+loop & 99.41 & [98.82, 99.83] & --- \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & exc+loop & 99.41 & [98.90, 99.80] & --- \\
loop\_only & loop compression & 85.63 & [83.53, 87.56] & 2 \\
full\_trace & complete trace & 81.76 & [79.70, 83.90] & --- \\
no\_trace & none & 75.13 & [72.77, 77.48] & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Component ablation on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). Tier~1 signals individually achieve near-perfect accuracy; combining them (VOTA) slightly dilutes performance.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Two findings stand out.
First, the Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{ae\_only} (99.92\%) and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) are not distinguishable ($p{=}0.80$, paired bootstrap, $B{=}10{,}000$), and both exceed VOTA (99.41\%, $p{=}0.01$ for \texttt{exception\_only} vs.\ VOTA, paired bootstrap).
This implies that combining signals in VOTA introduces minor noise rather than complementary information.
Second, removing assertion points from VOTA has no effect (VOTA\_no\_ae = VOTA = 99.41\%), confirming that within the VOTA mixture, exception events dominate the prediction signal.

Tier~2 signal \texttt{loop\_only} (85.63\%) improves over \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%) by 10.50pp ($p{<}0.0001$, bootstrap 95\% CI $[{+}8.24, {+}12.86]$), showing that loop compression captures some execution semantics, but far less than exception events.

\subsection{Information Density Decomposition}
\label{sec:density}

The gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) and VOTA (99.41\%) is 17.65pp.
We decompose this gap into two mechanisms by introducing an intermediate condition, \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}, which retains the complete trace as input but computes loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace tokens during training.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
\midrule
full\_trace & 81.76 & --- & --- \\
label\_only & 86.22 & +4.46pp & 26\% \\
VOTA & 99.41 & +17.65pp & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Information density decomposition. The full\_trace$\to$VOTA gap decomposes into gradient dilution (26\%, addressed by masking trace tokens from the loss) and information overload (74\%, addressed by removing irrelevant trace lines via VOTA compression).}
\label{tab:density}
\end{table}

As shown in Table~\ref{tab:density}, the decomposition attributes 26\% of the gap (+4.46pp, $p{<}0.0001$, bootstrap 95\% CI $[{+}2.35, {+}6.55]$) to \emph{gradient dilution}---the training signal is diluted across trace tokens that do not contribute to verdict prediction---and 74\% (+13.19pp) to \emph{information overload}---the model must process trace lines irrelevant to the fault at inference time.
This two-factor decomposition is consistent across models: the VOTA cross-model gap (14.96pp, Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is confounded by training-time trace truncation on DeepSeek (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}), which amplifies information overload by removing diagnostic trace content from the majority of training samples.

\subsection{Calibration Analysis}
\label{sec:calibration}

Beyond accuracy, we evaluate whether trace conditions affect prediction calibration, motivated by recent findings that code LLM confidence is often poorly calibrated \citep{spiess2025calibration}.
Figure~\ref{fig:calibration} shows reliability diagrams for four conditions on Qwen-2.5-7B.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{ECE $\downarrow$} & \textbf{Brier $\downarrow$} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & \textbf{0.0004} & \textbf{0.0008} \\
exception\_only & 0.003 & 0.0013 \\
VOTA & 0.005 & 0.005 \\
full\_trace & 0.096 & 0.144 \\
no\_trace & 0.171 & 0.197 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Calibration metrics on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). ECE = expected calibration error; Brier = Brier score. Lower is better for both.}
\label{tab:calibration}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:calibration} shows that calibration quality mirrors the Tier~1/2 hierarchy.
Tier~1 conditions (\texttt{ae\_only}: ECE=0.0004; \texttt{exception\_only}: ECE=0.003) produce near-perfectly calibrated predictions, while \texttt{full\_trace} (ECE=0.096) and \texttt{no\_trace} (ECE=0.171) exhibit substantial miscalibration.
VOTA (ECE=0.005) is well-calibrated but slightly worse than either Tier~1 component alone, reinforcing the pattern that combining trace signals dilutes rather than improves the prediction signal.

The Brier scores tell a consistent story: \texttt{ae\_only} (0.0008) and \texttt{exception\_only} (0.0013) achieve near-zero scores, while \texttt{no\_trace} (0.197) indicates substantial miscalibration.

Figure~\ref{fig:cross_model_gap} visualizes the cross-model gap pattern, showing that exception-based conditions maintain tight cross-model agreement while VOTA and lower-tier conditions diverge.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig2_calibration}
\caption{Reliability diagrams for four trace conditions on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). The Tier~1 condition (\texttt{exception\_only}) clusters near the diagonal (well-calibrated), while \texttt{full\_trace} and \texttt{no\_trace} exhibit systematic overconfidence.}
\label{fig:calibration}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
\caption{Cross-model accuracy gap (Qwen $-$ DeepSeek) across trace conditions. Exception-based signals transfer across models (0.50pp gap), while VOTA is model-dependent (14.96pp gap).}
\label{fig:cross_model_gap}
\end{figure}

\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first systematic study of what execution trace components drive verdict prediction performance.
Through component ablation across two code LLMs, we established three findings:

\textbf{(1) Exception signal transfer.}
Exception events alone achieve 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 on Qwen (3 seeds) and 99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds, with one outlier at 91.09\% from LoRA initialization sensitivity.
Even the outlier exceeds VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp, confirming exception events as the most effective component across models; training stability is a secondary factor for smaller models.
In contrast, the full VOTA representation degrades by 14.96pp on DeepSeek---a gap confounded by training-time trace truncation (the majority of DeepSeek VOTA samples exceed the context window; \S\ref{sec:cross_model}) and model capability differences, which cannot be disentangled in the current design.

\textbf{(2) Information density decomposition.}
The 17.65pp gap between full traces and VOTA decomposes into gradient dilution (26\%, from training on irrelevant trace tokens) and information overload (74\%, from processing irrelevant trace lines at inference).
The primary bottleneck is trace content selection, not loss design.

\textbf{(3) Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy.}
Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy, while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) reach 85.6\%.
Combining tiers in VOTA slightly degrades performance (99.41\%), confirming that additional trace components introduce noise rather than complementary signal.

These results yield a practical design principle: for verdict prediction, extract the highest-specificity diagnostic signal and discard everything else.
Future work should test whether exception dominance extends to other datasets (DebugBench, LiveCodeBench), model scales, and classification tasks beyond verdict prediction.

\label{sec:setup}

\subsection{Task Definition}
\label{sec:task}

We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a code snippet $c$, a test input $i$, and an expected output $o_{\text{exp}}$, predict whether executing $c$ on $i$ produces $o_{\text{exp}}$.
Let $\mathbf{x} = (c, i, o_{\text{exp}})$ denote the static context and $t$ the full execution trace obtained by running $c(i)$.
Each experimental condition defines a trace preprocessing function $f$ such that the model receives $(\mathbf{x}, f(t))$ and generates a verdict $\hat{y} \in \{\text{pass}, \text{fail}\}$.

We formulate verdict prediction as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in an instruction-tuned chat format.
The model generates a single token---\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}---as its response, which constitutes a single token in both the Qwen and DeepSeek tokenizers used in our experiments.
This setup differs fundamentally from code generation: the output space is $O(1)$, so all task-relevant information must be extracted from the input representation.
The trace preprocessing function $f$ is therefore the primary design variable.

\subsection{Dataset}
\label{sec:dataset}

We use the verdict prediction dataset constructed by \cite{placeholder_WangEMNLP2025} from CRUXEval \citep{placeholder_GuICML2024}, a benchmark of 800 standalone Python functions designed for execution reasoning evaluation.
\cite{placeholder_WangEMNLP2025} paired each function with multiple test cases and collected line-by-line execution traces via a Python tracer, recording every executed line, variable assignment, function call, and exception event.
This produced 5{,}910 labeled examples, each containing the source code, test input, expected output, ground-truth verdict, and full execution trace.

We split the data into 4{,}720 training and 1{,}190 test examples.
The test set is pass-dominant: 71.51\% of samples have verdict \emph{pass}, establishing a majority-class baseline of 71.51\% accuracy.
This class imbalance motivates our use of per-class precision, recall, and F1 alongside overall accuracy.

\subsection{Trace Representations}
\label{sec:vota}

\paragraph{Full trace.}
The raw execution trace records every line execution, variable state, and function call in sequential order.
For models with limited context, traces are tokenized and truncated to fit a 2{,}048-token window.
We apply chat-template-aware truncation that reserves token budget for the verdict label at the sequence end, preventing the label from being right-truncated during tokenization---a failure mode that causes complete training collapse (Appendix~\ref{app:truncation}).

\paragraph{VOTA.}
Variable-Outcome Trace Abstraction (VOTA) extracts three diagnostic components from the full trace:

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=4pt]
\item \textbf{Exception summary.}
Structured error events in the format \texttt{[ERROR] type: \textit{ExceptionType} message: \textit{msg}}.
Present only when execution raises an exception; absent for successful runs.

\item \textbf{Assertion point.}
A snapshot of the actual and expected output values: \texttt{[ASSERT] expected: \textit{X} actual: \textit{Y}}.
Captures the diagnostic moment where the execution outcome can be compared against the specification.

\item \textbf{Loop compression.}
A behavioral summary replacing repetitive per-iteration trace lines with iteration count and variable change trends (e.g., \texttt{3 iterations, result grows [2] $\to$ [2,4] $\to$ [2,4,6]}).
\end{enumerate}

VOTA is not a lossy compression of the full trace.
It performs \emph{targeted extraction}: each component isolates a specific diagnostic signal while discarding all intermediate execution state.
Prior trace compression work optimizes for generation fluency by retaining a narrative of execution \citep{placeholder_FerrandoArXiv2025,placeholder_TraceCoderICSE2026}; VOTA instead selects the minimal set of events sufficient for a binary judgment.
Figure~\ref{fig:vota_example} illustrates the transformation.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\columnwidth}{%
\small
\textbf{Full trace} (excerpt, 847 tokens):\\[2pt]
\texttt{L2: x = [1, 2, 3]}\\
\texttt{L3: result = []}\\

\texttt{L5: ~~result.append(item * 2)}\\
\texttt{L4: for item in x: ~~\# iter 2}\\
\texttt{L5: ~~result.append(item * 2)}\\

\texttt{~~grows [2] $\to$ [2,4] $\to$ [2,4,6]}\\
\texttt{[ASSERT] expected: [2,4,6]}\\
\texttt{~~~~~~~~ actual: [2,4,6]}\\
\texttt{[No exception]}}}

\label{fig:vota_example}
\end{figure}

\label{sec:conditions}

\end{table}

Gradient checkpointing is enabled for all runs.

All experiments run on 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs (96\,GB each) with CUDA 12.8.
Each single-GPU training run completes in approximately 2 hours.

Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap tests on per-sample predictions.
We additionally report per-class precision, recall, and F1, as well as expected calibration error \citep[ECE;][]{placeholder_NaeiniICML2015} and Brier score to assess prediction confidence.
